name: Karnak
info: Karnak is the vast complex of temples, pylons and chapels near Luxor in Egypt, begun under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and added to for centuries, the main place of worship of the Theban Triad headed by Amun.

facts.made: Built over many centuries by about thirty pharaohs, from Senusret I of the Middle Kingdom into the Ptolemaic Kingdom, though most surviving buildings date from the New Kingdom; later cultures adapted some of its buildings for their own worship
facts.form: A mix of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings in four main parts: the Precincts of Amun-Re, Mut and Montu and the dismantled Temple of Amenhotep IV; the Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 columns on an area of 5,000 square metres
facts.where: Near Luxor in Egypt, beside the modern village of el-Karnak, 2.5 kilometres north of Luxor; part of the monumental city of Thebes, listed by UNESCO in 1979
facts.known: the Great Hypostyle Hall with its 134 columns; Hatshepsut's obelisks; the Red Chapel; the Avenue of Sphinxes to Luxor Temple; a building history of some thirty pharaohs; Coptic churches founded among the ruins; the sacred precincts of Amun-Re, Mut and Montu

t: Karnak was the ancient Egyptian Ipet-isut, 'The Most Selected of Places', and the main place of worship of the Theban Triad, with the god Amun as its head.

Construction began under Senusret I in the Middle Kingdom and continued into the Ptolemaic Kingdom; about thirty pharaohs contributed, which gave the complex a size, complexity and diversity not seen elsewhere.

After the closing of pagan temples in the Roman Empire, Karnak was mostly abandoned and Christian churches were founded among the ruins; Europeans described it from 1589, and it was listed by UNESCO with the rest of Thebes in 1979.
dyk: Hatshepsut had twin obelisks erected at the entrance to the temple; one still stands, and the other has toppled and is broken.
ev: Construction at the complex began during the reign of Senusret I (1971–1926 BCE) in the Middle Kingdom; Thebes later became the capital of the unified country, and almost every pharaoh of the Eighteenth Dynasty added something to the site
Constantius II ordered the closing of pagan temples throughout the Roman Empire, and Karnak, by then mostly abandoned, received Christian churches among its ruins
An unknown Venetian wrote the first European description of the temple complex, without giving it a name
Two Capuchin missionary brothers travelled through the area, and the name Karnak is first attested as a village name and the name of the complex
Paul Lucas published the first drawing of Karnak, which is rather inaccurate
Karnak was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List along with the rest of the city of Thebes

sections.origins:
The history of the Karnak complex is largely the history of Thebes and its changing role in the culture. Religious centres varied by region, and when a new capital of the unified culture was established, the religious centres in that area gained prominence. The city of Thebes does not appear to have been of great significance before the Eleventh Dynasty, and earlier temple building there would have been relatively small, with shrines dedicated to the early deities of Thebes, the earth goddess Mut and Montu. Early building was destroyed by invaders.

The earliest known artefact found in the area of the temple is a small, eight-sided column from the Eleventh Dynasty, which mentions Amun-Re. Amun, sometimes called Amen, was long the local tutelary deity of Thebes. He was identified with the ram and the goose, and his name means 'hidden' or 'the hidden god'. Construction at the complex began during the reign of Senusret I, who reigned 1971–1926 BCE, in the Middle Kingdom. Major construction in the Precinct of Amun-Re took place in the Eighteenth Dynasty, when Thebes became the capital of the unified country.
sections.content:
Karnak comprises a vast mix of temples, pylons, chapels and other buildings. It has four main parts: the Precinct of Amun-Re, the Precinct of Mut, the Precinct of Montu and the dismantled Temple of Amenhotep IV. The term Karnak is often understood as the Precinct of Amun-Re only. That is the largest precinct and is dedicated to Amun-Re, the chief deity of the Theban Triad. It holds several colossal statues, including a figure of Pinedjem I that is 10.5 metres tall, and one of the largest obelisks, weighing 328 tons and standing 29 metres tall.

The Great Hypostyle Hall in this precinct has an area of 5,000 square metres with 134 massive columns arranged in 16 rows. One hundred and twenty-two of them are 10 metres tall, and the other 12 are 21 metres tall with a diameter of over 3 metres. The sun god's shrine was built so that light is focused upon it during the winter solstice. The Precinct of Mut, to the south, was dedicated to the mother goddess Mut, identified in the Eighteenth Dynasty as the wife of Amun-Re, and has its own crescent-shaped sacred lake. The Precinct of Montu, to the north, honours the war god Montu, the son of Mut and Amun-Re, and is much smaller.
sections.making:
Thutmose I erected an enclosure wall connecting the Fourth and Fifth pylons, which make up the earliest part of the temple still standing in situ. Hatshepsut had monuments constructed and restored the original Precinct of Mut, which had been ravaged by the foreign rulers during the Hyksos occupation. She also had the twin obelisks erected, and her Red Chapel, intended as a barque shrine, may originally have stood between them. She later ordered two more obelisks to mark her sixteenth year as pharaoh; one broke during construction, so a third was made to replace it. The broken one remains at its quarry in Aswan as the unfinished obelisk, which shows how obelisks were quarried.

Construction of the Great Hypostyle Hall may have begun in the Eighteenth Dynasty, although most new building was undertaken under Seti I and Ramesses II in the Nineteenth. The sandstone for the Precinct of Amun-Re, including all the columns, was brought from Gebel Silsila, 100 miles south on the Nile. The architraves on the columns are estimated to weigh 70 tons. They may have been lifted with levers, or towed up ramps of sand, mud, brick or stone; a common alternative theory favours the ramps. An unfinished pillar shows that final carving was done after the drums were in place.
sections.reception:
Karnak is distinguished from most other Egyptian temples by the length of time over which it was developed and used. Approximately thirty pharaohs contributed to the buildings. Few of its individual features are unique, but their size and number are vast, and the deities represented range from some of the earliest worshipped to some of those worshipped much later in Egyptian history. Merneptah of the Nineteenth Dynasty commemorated his victories over the Sea Peoples on the walls of the Cachette Court, the start of the processional route, also called the Avenue of Sphinxes, to Luxor Temple.

Not every ruler built in the same spirit. Akhenaten, or Amenhotep IV, built a temple east of the main complex, outside the walls of the Amun-Re precinct. He had attempted to overcome the powerful priesthood that had gained control over Egypt before his reign. The temple was destroyed immediately after his death and so thoroughly demolished that its full extent and layout are unknown. The priesthood regained its position as soon as he died and was instrumental in destroying many records of his existence. Ancient Greek and Roman writers wrote about monuments in Upper Egypt and Nubia, Karnak among them.
sections.survival:
The last major change to the layout of the Precinct of Amun-Re was the addition of the First Pylon and the massive enclosure walls around the precinct, both built by Nectanebo I of the Thirtieth Dynasty. In 323 CE the Roman emperor Constantine the Great recognised the Christian religion, and in 356 Constantius II ordered the closing of pagan temples throughout the Roman Empire, into which Egypt had been annexed in 30 BCE. Karnak was by then mostly abandoned. Christian churches were founded among the ruins; the most famous example is the reuse of the central hall of the Festival Hall of Thutmose III, where painted decorations of saints and Coptic inscriptions can still be seen.

The exact position of Thebes was unknown in medieval Europe, although Herodotus and Strabo both give it. Several European authors of the 15th and 16th centuries who visited only Lower Egypt put Thebes in or near Memphis. The first European description of the complex was by an unknown Venetian in 1589. The name Karnak is first attested in 1668, in the travels of the Capuchin brothers Protais and Charles François d'Orléans. Paul Lucas's drawing of 1704 mixed the Precincts of Amun-Re and Montu. Later visitors included Richard Pococke, James Bruce and scientists of the Napoleon expedition, among them Vivant Denon, in 1798–1799.
sections.legacy:
In 1979 Karnak was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List along with the rest of the monumental city of Thebes. It takes its modern name from the nearby village of el-Karnak, which means 'fortified village', in place of the ancient name Ipet-isut. Its long history has made it a record of adaptation, since later cultures used the buildings of the ancient Egyptians for their own religious purposes, as in the Coptic churches.

Research there has continued. Betsy Bryan led a Johns Hopkins University team that excavated and restored the Precinct of Mut, where six hundred black granite statues were found in the courtyard of the temple. In 2006 she presented findings about a festival that included apparent intentional overindulgence in alcohol, in which the priestesses and the population took part, and historical records speak of tens of thousands attending. The festival is linked to the myth of Sekhmet, whom Ra tricked into drinking beer mixed with pomegranate juice that looked like blood. In 2009 UCLA launched a website dedicated to virtual reality digital reconstructions of the complex and other resources.

summary: Karnak, near Luxor in Egypt, is a vast complex of temples, pylons and chapels begun under Senusret I and added to by about thirty pharaohs into Ptolemaic times. It was the main place of worship of the Theban Triad headed by Amun, and later served Christian communities.
references: Elizabeth Blyth, Karnak: Evolution of a Temple (Routledge, 2006)
notes: The article contradicts itself on the Precinct of Mut: the Overview says it is closed to the public and not yet restored, while the Main parts section says it has been opened after Johns Hopkins excavation and restoration. Public access left out.
The Overview says Hatshepsut destroyed and partially restored the original Precinct of Mut, while the History says it was ravaged by the Hyksos and restored by her; the History version is used.
Start year: the article gives Senusret I's reign as 1971–1926 BCE and says construction began during it, not in a given year; -1971 used with circa true.
Events 18th, 19th and 30th Dynasty carry no years because the article gives none for them.
The article calls Karnak the second-most-visited site in Egypt; left out as a ranking.
The Hypostyle Hall's construction method is given as theory only (levers or ramps); the article's mention of experiments elsewhere is left out.
The article's description of the Mut myth places Sekhmet's story in a later myth developed around the festival; kept short.
